topic: DGX Spark firmware update: synthetic burn test down about 11% while real LLM serving got 4% to 8% faster
title: The Benchmark Lied
description: Working description; the package stage overwrites this. What the DGX Spark firmware update actually did to benchmarks and to real model serving.
hook_candidates: You updated your Spark. The benchmark lied.
Your benchmark says slower. Your models say faster.
DGX Spark update: burn test says slower, serving says faster
The burn test lied to you. Your DGX Spark got faster.
Synthetic benchmarks lie to your DGX Spark
You benchmarked the wrong thing tonight.
DGX Spark firmware: same watts, less math, faster models
Faster where it matters. Slower where it shows.
Trust the burn test and you will skip a faster Spark.
The benchmark every Spark owner runs is the wrong one.
narration_full: You updated your DGX Spark, and the benchmark lied. The Dashboard prompted, you clicked yes, then you checked the machine. You ran the GPU burn test, a quick synthetic stress run, to make sure nothing broke. The score came back lower. Same machine, same room, lower number. A burn test measures peak sixteen-bit math, the chip's top speed on a synthetic matrix trick, for a few seconds. Nothing about serving a model. Then a field report landed. A lab called Petronella updated its whole fleet of machines built on the chip inside your Spark. The burn dropped about eleven percent on every unit. Clocks the same or higher, watts the same. No throttling. But the lab measured what you actually do: serving. Decode, the part that writes your answer one word at a time, sped up. It went from twenty-three point one tokens a second to twenty-five with just you asking. Faster at every load. Here the lab offers a hypothesis, not a finding. Picture a kitchen. The chef chops instantly, but every ingredient arrives through one narrow doorway. The chef is your compute, the doorway is the memory bus, your unified memory, and the ingredients are the model's weights. To write one word, it reads the active weights out of memory. Not think. Read. The honest catch. Prefill, the part that reads your whole prompt first, runs on raw math like the burn. There the doorway breaks: reading your prompt is one big block of math. Prefill ran flat to a touch slower. Prompt-heavy work? That drop is real for you. Your moves. Step one: benchmark your real workload before you update, and note the tokens per second. Step two: run the firmware update itself. Step three: re-run the same workload a few times. Trust that pair, before and after. The burn said eleven percent slower. Your model said faster. Only one of those is what you feel.
